transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-10
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 63 minutes (scheduled)
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Leah Chen (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendes (MercuryTrade CTO), Priya Kapoor (Lead ML Engineer), Dmitri Ivanov (SRE)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be incomplete):
- POC scope: 3 weeks, focus on throughput and latency characterization.
- Data: customer will share anonymized request traces and prompt corpus.
- Benchmarks: run hosted baseline, then dedicated GPU pool; measure p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, and cost per 1k tokens.

Transcript:
[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Samir from Redwood, AE on this account, and with me is Leah our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Carlos: Good, thanks. Quick intro — I'm Carlos, CTO. Priya's our lead on ML and Dmitri runs infra.
[00:11] Priya: Hi all.
[00:13] Leah: Great to meet you. Quick agenda — we want to align on your workload, targets (QPS/concurrency), success criteria, and a realistic POC timeline. Then we'll propose a benchmark plan.
[00:22] Carlos: Sounds good. For context, MercuryTrade does real-time trade commentary and risk alerts. We have a stream of trade events that trigger a prompt to an LLM to generate a short summary + suggested action. Typical payloads are small but output can vary.
[00:35] Priya: Our current prod flow calls an internal model via SageMaker endpoint; it's okay but costy and latency is inconsistent. We're evaluating Redwood for a POC to see if we can get better tail latency and lower token costs.
[00:46] Samir: Perfect. Can you share rough numbers for QPS and concurrency?
[00:50] Priya: Average QPS right now is about 2.5 requests/sec, but during market open we spike to around 60 QPS for a 15-20 minute window. Concurrency wise we see up to 120 concurrent in flight during spikes.
[01:05] Leah: Helpful — so baseline avg 2-3 QPS and peak 60 sustained for short windows, with 120 concurrent. Do you have distribution of input/output token lengths?
[01:14] Priya: Yes, typical input token length is small — median about 40 tokens, 75th around 120. Outputs average 220 tokens, 95th about 780 tokens (when we include long risk analysis).
[01:26] Dmitri: Just to add, our SLA requires p95 end-to-end under 800ms for these alerts; anything above that triggers escalations. Cost target is roughly $0.015 per 1k output tokens if possible, but that's negotiable.
[01:40] Samir: Okay noted. Two quick clarifications: is the 120 concurrency mainly due to streaming of long responses, or multiple independent requests queued?
[01:48] Priya: It's a mix. Some clients fan-out multiple prompts in parallel; plus long outputs increase holding time.
[01:55] Leah: For the POC we usually model both the QPS arrival process and token distribution. We'll want your traces — ideally captures with timestamps and request/response token counts. That helps us build a traffic model and simulate bursts.
[02:07] Priya: We can extract two weeks of anonymized traces. We'll scrub PII before sending.
[02:12] Samir: Great. On the benchmarks: typical Redwood POC approach is week 1 ingest traces and run hosted baseline (we run your prompts against our hosted API), week 2 run dedicated capacity tests (we provision a dedicated pool approximating target concurrency), week 3 iterate and tune (batching, KV caching, quantization) and final report. Does that align with your timeline expectations?
[02:30] Carlos: Yes, that's reasonable. We want the baseline numbers quickly so we can compare to the SageMaker endpoint.
[02:36] Leah: We'll aim to provide a baseline report with p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, and cost estimates by the end of week 1. For the dedicated run in week 2 we'll target the peak window and test sustained 60 QPS and stress up to 120 concurrency to see how tails behave.
[02:50] Priya: For the baselines, can you also measure token-level latency? We want to see per-token generation time since some of our functions stream partial responses.
[02:58] Leah: Yes, we capture per-token throughput and overall time to first token as well. Small note — streaming behavior can slightly increase p95 because of chunking, but it usually helps user-perceived latency.
[03:10] Samir: One more thing on cost: we'll include both hosted billing numbers and an estimated unit cost for running on a dedicated pool (includes reserved GPU amortized, kernel optimizations, and batching). We'll surface how batching and prefix caching reduce cost per token for repetitive prompts.
[03:24] Carlos: Good. Security — we need SOC2 and encryption details. For the hosted baseline, what data retention and logs do you keep?
[03:32] Samir: Our hosted API retains logs for 30 days by default; we can offer options for shorter retention or no-training retention on an account basis. We'll share the Redwood security pack and SOC2 report.
[03:41] Dmitri: Also, network-wise we need to understand VPC peering options for the dedicated run. We prefer private connectivity for any production later.
[03:49] Leah: Dedicated supports VPC peering and private deployments; for POC we can do a temporary private link. We'll send the network diagram and steps. Apologies if I say it weird — sometimes our docs spell VPC as V-P-C in transcriptions.
[04:01] Priya: Fine. Back to workload: we have a couple of prompt families — quick summaries (~60 tokens out), and deep analysis (~700 tokens out). The deep ones are only ~10% of requests but dominate cost and tail latency.
[04:14] Leah: That's typical. In our modeling we weight the distribution and run separate scenarios: 'normal' mix and 'heavy' mix where deep analysis is 25% to stress tails.
[04:24] Samir: Can you share any constraints on accuracy/regression? I.e., what degree of output drift are you willing to tolerate compared to your current model?
[04:33] Priya: We need parity on factual correctness and style; small wording changes are okay but no hallucinations on trade positions. We'll include a small eval set to check quality during POC.
[04:43] Carlos: Also important: measurable metrics — p95 latency < 800ms (we said), and throughput that can handle the spike. Cost is a tie-breaker.
[04:50] Leah: Understood. For the dedicated runs we may suggest quantized model variants to reduce latency and cost — we'll propose a couple of model/config options and expected tradeoffs.
[04:59] Priya: Do you have historical numbers to show what p95 looks like at 60 QPS for similar customers?
[05:05] Samir: We can share anonymized benchmark summaries. Typical p95 for 300-800 token outputs at 60 QPS on a dedicated pool ranges 200–500ms depending on model and batching; hosted numbers are usually a bit higher due to multi-tenant variance. We'll include concrete examples in the baseline report.
[05:22] Dmitri: For benchmarking windows, we'd prefer the tests to run overnight (low-prod impact) and we'll provide a test account and keys.
[05:29] Leah: That works. We'll coordinate a 2-hour window for the heavy stress test.
[05:33] Priya: For tokenization — we use GPT tokenization for metrics; hope that's okay.
[05:38] Leah: Totally fine. We just need the token counts per request.
[05:42] Samir: Quick note on metrics to capture: requests/sec, concurrent requests, time to first token, time to last token, per-token throughput, GPU utilization, and cost breakdown (GPU hours + amortized infra).
[05:54] Carlos: Good list. Regarding success criteria — let's write them down: 1) functional parity on eval set, 2) p95 latency < 800ms for normal mix, 3) maintain throughput for 60 QPS and degrade gracefully up to 120 concurrency, 4) cost per 1k tokens below $0.02 as aspirational.
[06:15] Leah: I'll capture those as our POC acceptance criteria.
[06:19] Priya: On the topic of caching: do you support prefix or KV caching out of the box? Some of our prompts reuse large prefixes.
[06:26] Samir: Yes, Redwood supports prefix/KV caching on the runtime; we can enable it during the dedicated run and quantify the hit rate benefits. The term sometimes shows up as K-V cash in transcripts, but it's KV cache.
[06:37] Dmitri: For security sign-off we'll need SAML SSO, RBAC, and an audit log export. Do you have SSO options?
[06:44] Samir: We support SAML SSO, RBAC, and detailed audit logs. We'll share feature docs and what's available in hosted vs private.
[06:51] Carlos: Ok good. Any blockers on our side besides sending traces and network diagram?
[06:56] Priya: Need a short NDA addendum to cover sharing of some internal prompts — legal is okay with a limited addendum.
[07:02] Samir: We can sign a POC NDA addendum; I'll loop in our legal.
[07:06] Leah: Now let's sketch the benchmark plan detail. Step 0: ingest traces and build traffic model (Leah + Priya). Step 1: hosted baseline run (simulate normal and heavy mixes). Step 2: dedicated capacity run — provision GPU pool sized to expected concurrency and test sustained 60 QPS + spike to 120. Step 3: tuning — enable batching, KV caching, try quantized weights, and run A/B to measure accuracy delta. Step 4: final report and recommended deployment option.
[07:33] Priya: For the dedicated pool sizing, what's your rule-of-thumb for mapping concurrency and token lengths to number of GPUs?
[07:40] Leah: Very rough: for a 7B-style model quantized, you might get ~20-40 concurrent low-latency streams per A100 memory-optimized instance depending on sequence lengths. For 70B or unoptimized models it's much lower. We'll do an initial estimate once we see token distributions. We usually propose a conservative starting pool and then scale during tests.
[07:58] Samir: We'll include a sizing table in the SOW with conservative and optimized options.
[08:04] Carlos: Timeline recap — can you run hosted baseline this week? We need numbers to show execs by 12/20.
[08:12] Samir: We can run the hosted baseline by 12/17 if we get traces by 12/15 and the test account. That gives you a week to review before 12/20.
[08:20] Priya: We'll aim to deliver the traces by 12/15.
[08:23] Dmitri: We'll also share the network diagram and compliance items by 12/12.
[08:27] Samir: Great. On measurement thresholds — for the report we'll include p50/p95/p99 and cost per 1k tokens for both hosted and dedicated scenarios, plus sensitivity analysis for % deep-analysis requests.
[08:39] Leah: Also we'll log error rates and any 5xxs. If fallback is needed we can test multi-model routing so higher latency cases fall back to a cheaper variant or shorter response.
[08:50] Priya: That fallback idea is interesting — do you have automatic routing rules?
[08:53] Samir: Yes, routing policies can be set by latency, cost, or region; for POC we'll test manual routing but can demo automatic policies later.
[09:02] Carlos: Anything else on compliance?
[09:05] Dmitri: Just the SOC2 docs and encryption at rest + KMS details.
[09:09] Samir: We'll attach those to the follow-up email.
[09:12] Leah: One corner case — streaming long outputs can cause higher memory pressure in KV caches; we'll monitor GPU memory and tail latency.
[09:21] Priya: Alright. On evaluation, we'll provide a small golden set of prompts with expected key facts to check hallucinations.
[09:27] Samir: Perfect. We'll run quality checks post-benchmark and report any drift.
[09:31] Carlos: OK let's recap next steps.
[09:34] Samir: Recap: Redwood sends SOW + security pack by 12/12; MercuryTrade sends traces by 12/15 and network diagram by 12/12; Redwood runs hosted baseline by 12/17 and schedules dedicated window 12/18-12/19 for heavy stress test. Leah will coordinate exact times.
[09:49] Priya: Sounds good.
[09:50] Dmitri: Fine.
[09:51] Samir: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with calendar invites and the SOW.
[09:56] Carlos: Thanks, bye.

[END OF TRANSCRIPT - approx 63 minutes]

Notes on transcript quality: occasional mislabels and minor ASR errors (e.g., "K-V cash" instead of "KV cache", "SageMaker" sometimes butchered).

- Metrics to collect: p50/p95/p99 latency, time-to-first-token, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, cost per 1k tokens.
- POC acceptance criteria: functional parity on eval set, p95 < 800ms for normal mix, graceful degradation to 120 concurrency, aspirational cost target < $0.02 per 1k tokens.
